title: How To Actually Get Value Out of Tech Conferences
author: Artur Henriques
summary: Artur Henriques argues that business conferences are mainly networking events and that leaders should prepare deliberately rather than wander the booths. He recommends using the conference website or app to list existing partners attending, prioritising them, and booking short thirty-minute meetings in advance, including with senior decision-makers who are hard to reach otherwise. He then repeats the exercise for potential future partners, which can compress weeks of vendor discovery into a few days. On logistics he advises grouping meetings by hall, avoiding opening-hour slots and leaving buffers so one late meeting does not cascade. He adds practical advice on business-casual dress and comfortable shoes, behaving as if you have known people for years, and attending after-hours events where private dinners and candid insights happen. His measure of success is leaving with tools, contacts and information you can actually use. The piece suits Leadership as practical advice on stakeholder access and vendor negotiation.
points: Treat the conference as a networking event and pre-book thirty-minute meetings with prioritised existing partners, because many attendees fill their calendars well ahead.
Conferences give one-to-one access to CEO and CTO level decision-makers, which Henriques used to win extra services almost free of charge before a contract negotiation.
Meeting prospective vendors on site can compress weeks of procurement discovery into days, provided you arrive with practical use cases.
Cluster meetings by hall and leave buffers, since a single late meeting cascades through the day.
After-hours events and private dinners are where the most useful insight and access appear.
quotes: Conferences are more than just checking out new stuff the industry has to offer. It is mostly a business networking event, and anyone in a leadership role needs to prepare beforehand to capitalize on it.

The advantage of these conferences, is that you could reach out to key decision-making staff who also be attending. If you plan to negotiate better deals, or have some contract conditions reviewed, you can use these conferences to access higher-level decision-makers in one-to-one conversations.
For example, just before starting contract negotiations with a vendor, I got the CEO and the CTO of the company in a conference, to agree to add some extra services almost free of charge.
The important part is that you come out of these sessions with a clear idea of the product, technical landscape, drawbacks, advantages, and possible paths to do business together.
Conferences can be a great way to quickly assess a set of different vendors for a project the company might have in the pipeline. Weeks of discovery could be done in a few days.

If you are late to one meeting, that delay will likely cascade into every other meeting that follows. Avoid scheduling meetings very early in the morning, especially right when the doors open. Create buffers between blocks of meetings to give yourself breathing room.

Getting the branded pens and business cards is simply the way to start. A seasoned leader uses the conference as a way to facilitate access to other networking channels. For example, a private dinner with senior management from vendors or clients.
You know that you won the conference if you get away with tools, contacts, and information that you can actually use.
